# Decisions

Settled decisions, newest first. A decision here is not reopened without a
reason recorded as a new entry. Each says what was decided, when, and why —
the why matters more than the what, because it is what tells a later session
whether changed circumstances actually undermine the decision.

## 2026-09-19 — Item 6 stays open until a zip left behind by a failed run is removed too

**Chosen by the owner** ("option 2"), after item 6's closure test found one
narrow gap. The refresh copies the checked zip into the downloads folder and
then compares the two, but it records the zip as its own only after that
comparison. If the comparison failed, the zip would stay in the folder with
its copy never live: served to nobody, but a second try that day would
refuse until the file was removed by hand. **The fix is made before item 6
closes**: the refresh counts the zip as its own from the moment it is
copied in, so a failure after that removes it. It is made by a session other
than the one that ran item 6's test, and checked in strand 2's closure test
(item 7), not by the session that makes it.

**Why:** the change is two lines, and item 7 checks the refresh anyway, so
leaving a known gap in place would buy nothing. The session that tested the
code does not fix it and then mark its own fix.

**Fixed the same day** by a session that did not run item 6's test: one
line moved, then rehearsed on a scratch copy, including the planted
failure (`docs/STRAND-2-ITEM-6-BUILD.md`, "The gap fixed").

---

## 2026-09-19 — The refresh makes the zip before the copy goes live, and refuses a second copy on one day

**Agreed by the owner** ("proceed"), on `docs/STRAND-2-ITEM-6-BUILD.md`
(strand 2, item 6). A refresh builds the new copy and sets it aside, served
to nobody; makes its zip from it with the site's own login and program, and
checks it; puts the zip beside the live one; and only then puts the copy
live. If anything fails before that, what the run made is removed and
readers see nothing change. Two zips are kept, the live copy's and the one
before's, so the undo brings the old zip back with the old copy; the undo is
one command, `tools/refresh_copy.sh --undo --save`. **A second refresh on
the day of the live copy refuses**: undo the first, then refresh.

**Why:** made afterwards, the zip left a gap in which the download box
vanished, and would have stayed vanished if the zip failed. The date names
the copy, its zip and its lines of what changed, so two copies on one day
would give two different things one name.

## 2026-09-19 — The zip is made once from the copy, and handed over with the day downloaded

**The owner's decisions**, agreeing `docs/STRAND-2-ITEM-5-BUILD.md` with its
eight small choices as proposed. Built and live the same day.

- **Made once, not on each download.** A program reads the copy through the
  site's own login, which can only read, and writes the zip; it is kept in
  `/srv/downloads`, outside the site's releases, which the site can read and
  not write. Not backed up: it can be remade from the copy, and holds nothing
  about anyone. The site fills in "Downloaded on" as it hands it over;
  nothing else changes, and two readers the same day get the same file.
- **The address is the name**: `/download/legislativedata-2026-09-18.zip`.
  An older date's name goes to the Data page; a made-up name is not found.
- **No zip for the copy's date**: no download box, and the address gives
  part 6's "can't be shown right now". It can happen only if a refresh runs
  before item 6 teaches it to make the zip.
- **The CSV files**: commas, Windows line ends, UTF-8 with no marker,
  quotation marks only where needed, empty for empty; lines in the site's
  order where it has one, otherwise by the file's own columns; all 192 lines
  of sources.
- **The codebook**: "Worked out or read" on the four data files only; type
  as the copy stores it, with "yes or no" where the description begins
  "Yes"; the words from What the words mean by heading name.
- **The size on the link** to one decimal place of a megabyte (it reads
  0.1 MB today; the draft guessed 0.4); **the download day** is the UK's.

**Why made once:** it is checked before anyone gets it, and remade from the
same copy it is the same byte for byte, so the kept file is shown to be the
copy's. Item 6 then only has to make it at each refresh.

## 2026-09-19 — A monthly design and sanity sweep, once Phase 2 has closed

**The owner's decision**, signing off the table: **once Phase 2 closes, the
site gets a design and sanity sweep every month.** The owner brings what they
have noticed from using the site; the session goes through every page as a
reader would (a phone's width, dark, light, printing) and lists what is off;
the changes are agreed before any is made, and placed in whatever plan is open
then. **Until Phase 2 closes, the owner gives feedback as it comes**, and each
piece is placed in the build plan with their agreement before it is worked on,
as the plan already requires.

**Why:** the owner wants to judge the site after using it for a while, not
only at the moment a piece is signed off. A sweep at the end of each strand
was put to them and not taken: a monthly rhythm after the phase suits using
the site more than a check tied to the build.

**What waits for the first sweep:** the owner signed off the table "for the
moment": the nine small choices in `docs/STRAND-2-ITEM-4-BUILD.md` stand, the
house style holds on it, and it stays one scroll rather than pages of 10, 100
or all. Each of these is looked at again in the first sweep. Until then they
are settled, and are not reopened without the owner raising it.

**Items 2, 3 and 4 of strand 2 are closed**: their tests run by a session that
built none of them, and the owner's part signed off (`CLOSURE-TESTS.md`).

access every login had by default (`db/server/001`, with its undo). The owner:
"only you and I, outwith the app itself".

**Why:** found while running the closure test of strand 2, item 1. The site
opens only what it needs, and this was the one place it could open something
it did not need, including making scratch tables. The default had been taken
away for the accounts and never for this database.

## 2026-09-18 — The site reads the copy: how, and what it may not reach

**The owner's decisions** on `docs/STRAND-2-THE-SITE-READS-THE-COPY.md`
(strand 2, item 1), yes to all four:
- **A deploy refuses to go live if the site cannot read the copy.** The
  health check asks for the copy's `about` file as well as the accounts.
- **Postico's login keeps reading `previous`**, so the owner can look at the
  old copy before an undo. The site's login may not: the refresh takes it off
  `previous` as it renames, and the undo gives it back to what becomes live.
- **Three site releases are kept**: the live one and the two before it that
  were live. A release only staged, or failed, goes.
- **The site's way into the copy is deployed on its own**, before any page
  uses it, because it is a change to who can read what.

**Why:** settled 17 September that the site's login to the copy only reads,
proved by a check; the renaming of `live` to `previous` carries a permission
with it, found while laying this out, so the site's access is taken off at
that moment rather than trusted not to be used.

## 2026-09-18 — Nothing waits on a clock

**The owner's decision**, at the opening of the session after strand 1's
closure test was written. That test said it could not run until the nightly
backup of 19 September had finished, and "Now" put strand 2 behind it, so a
whole evening had nothing to do. The owner: "we should NOT be blocked by a
timed activity."

**A check that needs a scheduled job's output runs the job by hand**, the way
its timer does (`systemctl start <unit>`), and reads that run. A run started by
hand is the same script, and proves the same thing. Where a job cannot be run
by hand, the check is carried beside the next piece of work, not in front of
it.

**Why:** a check that waits for a timer blocks everything behind it for a
reason that has nothing to do with the work. Running the backup by hand costs
half a minute; retention keeps one copy a day, so an extra run loses nothing
older.

**What it does not change:** a strand still closes only when its closure test
has been run by another session.

- **A removed line is listed**, one line each, with its heading "(line

`tools/put_back_previous.sql`. Rehearsed in full the same day.

## 2026-09-18 — Every published figure is worked out from the published data, by working a reader can run

**Settled by the owner**, on finding 1 of `docs/BUILD-PLAN-CHECK.md`.

**The principle.** Every figure a reader sees is worked out in the published
database, from the published files, by working written in the reader's own
column names. The text shown beside a figure is the text that produced it, and
a reader can run it unchanged on their download and get the same numbers, or
change it and get their own. The working database holds the facts and checks
them before anything is published. No published figure is worked out there.

**Not both.** One version of each sum, never a working version and a reader's
version side by side, as ruled on 17 September. This settles what the 17
September entries left pulling two ways: "added in the same place" as the
existing calculations is now the published database, and "the calculation a
reader downloads" is the one that ran.

**What it changes.** The days between stages, the one figure published today,
is worked out in the working database, and only its answers are copied across.
It moves to the published database and is proved by rebuilding all 1657 lines
and comparing them cell by cell with today's before anything else changes. That
comes before the refresh is built. Every chart's working is written against the
published files from the start.

**Why.** It has always been a principle of this project that a researcher has
the data and can run the same calculations we did, or different ones. The data
was always published in full, stage dates included. What did not meet the
principle was the working: it was written in the working database's names,
which a reader never has.

**The working database's own sums** are not removed yet. What uses them is
listed for the owner in `STATE.md`, and each goes only once nothing needs it.

## 2026-09-18 — A quarter begins at the first whole day inside it

**Every part settled by the owner** in `docs/BLOCK-2-QUARTER-BOUNDARY.md`, on
the rule agreed on 17 September: a bill introduced on the day a quarter begins
counts in that quarter.

**Option A.** A bill's place is the days from its session's first meeting to
its introduction, divided by the days from that meeting to the session's last
day (or expected last day, M14); its quarter is `INT(4 × place) + 1`, and the
last day is the fourth. A quarter usually begins partway through a day (18 of
the 21 boundaries across the seven sessions), and a bill on that day goes in
the earlier quarter. **Why:** it is the plain arithmetic, so any reader with
the dates can check it. Under either reading no bill moves; none falls on any
of the 21 days.

**Nothing in the database changes, and no note changes now.** The rule is
written in `docs/PHASE-2-CALCULATIONS.md`, chart 5, where thought 5's
calculation reads it. The sentence for readers is settled there and goes into
thought 5's methodology note when that is written; a note cannot carry it
sooner, because the copy has no quarter heading for it to name. Thought 5's own
checklist adds the check that every bill is in exactly one quarter.

## 2026-09-17 — The notes name the published headings, in plain prose, and applies_to does not move

**The owner's decisions**, and what was built on them. Thirteen of the fourteen
methodology notes are rewritten to name the published copy's column headings, as

column.

**Shown as changes, not as fourteen whole notes.** The owner asked why they
needed to reread all fourteen. They did not. Twenty-one passages change only by
a heading being named, and were shown as a table of old and new wording; seven
change by more, and were the whole of what the owner read. All seven agreed.
*The general point:* a change to a body of settled text is reviewed as its
changes. Handing over every word of it again is not thoroughness, it is a way of
not being read.

**The notes carry no markup.** The proposal showed headings in backticks so the
owner could see them at a glance; what went into the database is plain prose. A

note carries the list of columns it bears on. Changing that list to published

against the column it describes, and the owner is the check on every claim this
project makes. So one mapping of working column to published heading is written
once and does two jobs: it builds the copy, and it translates this list. *What
would reopen it:* nothing foreseen; two lists from one mapping is fewer things
to keep in step than two lists kept by hand.

date_ended", sat after the sentence about Stage 3 and could be read as though

passages read back inside the transaction and the database read again after it,
then applied and all thirteen notes compared word for word against the approved
file. The closure test is written and unrun; a later session runs it.

## 2026-09-17 — The published copy's headings, and three of them settled by name

**The owner's decisions**, block 1 of `PHASE-2-CHARTS-BUILD.md`, point 2. The
nine files and every heading are proposed in `docs/PHASE-2-PUBLISHED-COPY.md`
and are not built. Three headings were put to the owner and all three settled
as proposed.

**`third_stage`, not `final_stage`.** The column holds a bill's third stage,
which is Stage 3 for a public or Hybrid Bill and Final Stage for a Private
Bill. Heading it `final_stage`, as the working database's view does, puts a
Private Bill's actual stage name at the top of a column whose cells sometimes
hold that very phrase, which invites a researcher to read the heading as a
claim about the stage rather than about its place in the sequence. `stage_3`
was refused for being wrong for the 24 Private Bills. *What would reopen it:*
nothing foreseen; the alternative names are both wrong for a class of bills
that exists.

**`enactment_status` is kept**, the one heading that is our vocabulary rather
than the Parliament's, because it fits all four of its values.
`became_an_act` was refused for reading as a yes-or-no question that "Blocked"
and "Pending" do not answer, and `act_status` for saying "the Act's status"
about bills that never became Acts. The dictionary file defines it.

**`bill_type_grouped` is carried**, so a researcher counting government bills
gets M4's grouping without having had to read M4, while the bill's own type
still reads Hybrid Bill. Leaving the grouping to the reader was considered and
refused on that ground. *What would reopen it:* a decision to drop the Forth
Crossing Bill's own choice from the outcomes chart, which is a separate open
question about the same bill.

**None of the three changes a cell.** Every value in the published copy stays
exactly as the Parliament names it — "Stage 3", "Final Stage", "Preliminary
Stage" — and nothing about the stage names is abstracted. These are the words
at the top of three columns, which appear in the top row of each CSV, in the
codebook, quoted inside the methodology notes, and on the site, where there is
no separate display-label layer.

**Found while doing it:** the allowed-value definitions that still name
database columns are nine entries across seven lists, not the four lists
`STATE.md` records. A way to settle it is proposed in §7 of
`PHASE-2-PUBLISHED-COPY.md` and is not started.

## 2026-09-17 — The site has two sections: Data, and Insights

**The owner's decision**, while the plan for building the charts was being
agreed. Two sections, with links in the header, both behind the sign-in.

**Data** is where a reader downloads the dataset and reads the same data on
screen, as a table of every bill. **Insights** is our charts and tables, each
chart carrying a file of its own figures to download.

**Why the name**, in the owner's words: the charts and tables are what provides
insight into the raw data. "Charts" and "Findings" were offered as flatter
words and not taken.

**What it settles.** Where the table of every bill lives: it opens the Data
section, as a destination in its own right and not only the place a figure's
"show me the bills" arrives. The full dataset stays on Data; a chart's own
figures sit with the chart, which is the file beneath each chart already settled
earlier the same day.

## 2026-09-17 — The plan for turning the mock-ups into pages on the site

**The owner's decisions**, eight of them, taken one at a time on the plan in
`docs/PHASE-2-CHARTS-BUILD.md`. That file is the plan the build follows; this
records what was settled and why.

1. **The published copy is built first**, to what was settled on 17 September
   and no more. There is no version where a chart goes live first: the site is
   not permitted to open the working database.
2. **Its headings are chosen, and the methodology notes rewritten in them,
   before any chart calculation is written.** Otherwise six calculations are
   written twice. Both go to the owner.
3. **Every figure, for every choice, is worked out when the copy is taken.**
   Confirmed after sizing: about three thousand lines across all six charts.
   This closes the trigger recorded earlier the same day — that the choices
   might multiply past what can sensibly be worked out in advance.
4. **The table of every bill is built straight after the first chart**, not
   last, so no chart ships with a provenance promise it cannot keep.
5. **The charting library is served from the machine**, pinned, like the fonts.
6. **The mock-ups' three palettes become the site's**, subject to one check for
   colour-blindness and for dark and light, which has not been run. Anything
   failing it is adjusted and shown to the owner, and the result recorded, so
   charts two to six do not each reopen it.
7. **Three small items are cleared first**, each with its own checklist before
   it is built: "In progress" moves to the end of the order of outcomes, being
   not an ending, which breaks the tie with "Fell: financial resolution not
   agreed"; a bill introduced on the day a quarter begins counts in that
   quarter; M9 is left alone and M10's account of how its own rule came about is
   cut, to match the notes rewritten that day.
8. **The order of the six**, thought 2 first because it is already accepted and
   its figures are simplest, thought 5 last because it brings the most new
   machinery. Roughly ten sessions, the first three or four producing nothing
   visible.

**Why a general plan before building any of it**, in the owner's words: it lets
the common problems be seen at once rather than hit one at a time. It found
three — the page furniture repeated six times, dark and light, and the route
from a figure to its bills — which are now built once.

## 2026-09-17 — A mock-up is built only from what the database holds, and a figure is set beside what an even spread would give rather than labelled

**The owner's decision**, twice over, while thought 5 was being worked out.

**Only what the database holds.** A mock-up uses the data that is in the
database today. Where a question needs something that is not — the day each
session's dissolution or pre-election recess began, for instance — the
exploration is worth seeing, but it stops there and the dates go through the
gateway as a coding change before any chart rests on them. The owner: "we've
drifted … a bit away from what the db holds (which we agreed not to do …)".

**Helpers, not verdicts.** Where a chart asks whether something is evenly
spread or moving over time, it shows the measured figure beside what an even
spread would give, and a test of how often chance alone would produce a
difference that size. It does not label a session "front-loaded" or "centred",
as the owner's example screenshots do. The owner: "That will be driven by
objective stats and not subjective opinion. We don't need to use the same
metrics as the examples i showed you."

**What this gave, on thought 5:** no session's government bills are measurably
uneven across the quarters, and there is no trend across the sessions. The
expectation was that none would be found, and a result the other way would have
been just as publishable.

**What would reopen it:** a reader telling us the tests are unreadable, or a
question the database cannot answer that matters enough to add to it.

## 2026-09-17 — The charts are drawn with Apache ECharts

**The owner's decision**, answering the addition the drawing rule required.
**Apache ECharts**, Apache 2.0 licence, version 6.1.0 at the time of choosing.
Chosen over Chart.js because stacked bars, figures on bars, legends, hovering and
dark and light modes come without add-ons. The owner: charts will be a big
feature of the site from here on, so the tools should be the ones it needs.

**On the site it is served from the machine**, like the fonts, so a reader's

## 2026-09-17 — Charts use colour with a legend, readers choose through filters, and charts are drawn in the browser

**The owner's decisions**, on the three rules the step back reopened, each as
proposed in `docs/PHASE-2-CHARTS-RULES.md`.

**Colour.** On a chart, colour may tell things apart, in a palette of its own
readable with colour-blindness and in dark and light. Colour never stands
alone: a legend or label gives each its word, and the figure is shown. Colour
never grades: no green for passed, no red for fell. The accent still never
touches data, and in the downloads and the table of every bill an outcome is
still a word. **This changes** "Colour means one thing, and an outcome is a
word" (15 September) for charts only. The palette is chosen with the first
mock-up.

**What a reader can choose.** Each chart gives the choices its write-up
justifies, through filters and dropdowns, from a fixed list we set. It is not a
chart builder, which stays the playground's (`PLAN.md`). **This changes** the
two switches of 17 September; both remain available to a chart that needs them.

**How a chart is drawn.** In the reader's browser, so hovering gives a figure
and a choice redraws at once. Every figure, for every choice, is still worked
out in the database when the copy is taken, and the page only draws. The
charting library is an addition, put to the owner by name before it is used.
The date sits inside the chart's frame, and the one-sentence description is on
the chart itself. **This changes** "charts drawn on the machine" (17 September).

**Why:** the downloads stay plain and the charts may bring the data alive
(the entry below). **What would reopen it:** a chart whose colour or choices
get between a reader and what the data says.

## 2026-09-17 — The downloads stay plain, and the charts and tables may bring the data alive

**The owner's position**, taken on stepping back from the first draft of chart 1.
Two things are going on, with different jobs. **The downloads** are to be very
boring, in a good way: accurate, complete, with provenance. **The charts and
tables** cannot lose sight of that, but may try to make the data come alive, with
good formatting, presentation and colour. Doing both at once is one of the
things that sets the site apart.

**Why.** The first draft of chart 1 was built to rules written as if a chart had
to be as austere as a download, and it showed every combination at once: a grid
of 35 squares a reader could not take in. The owner's screenshots of another
project, for inspiration only, show what presentation can do without being
gimmicky, and a window into the data that banks of statistics do not give.

**What it does not change.** Everything about the downloads. And, for the
charts and tables: every number is worked out in the database and is the same
number a reader can download; a reader can go from a figure to its bills and
their provenance; every chart names its methodology notes and carries its date.
The screenshots are a reminder of why: the one listing the longest passages
gives the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Bill 1408 days, the impossible
figure `PLAN.md` cites.

**What it reopens.** The presentation rules applied to the charts as if they
were downloads: colour (15 September), the two switches, and charts drawn on the
machine as fixed images (both 17 September). What replaces each is put to the
owner in `docs/PHASE-2-CHARTS-RULES.md`, and nothing changes until they decide.

**What would reopen this:** a chart or table whose presentation gets between a
reader and what the data says, or a figure on a chart that a reader cannot
trace to the download.

## 2026-09-17 — A running session is measured to its expected last day, kept in a cell of its own

**The owner's decision**, answering the list of calculations: chart 5, bills
introduced in each quarter of a session, measures Session 7 to an estimated last
day, and says so upfront. All nine parts of the change were then laid out and
approved together, with the wording of M14 and of chart 5's opening sentence
(`docs/PHASE-2-CALCULATIONS.md`, last section). Built the same day as `db/104`.

**The date is 1 April 2031, worked out from the law.** The next poll is due on
the first Thursday in May 2031, 1 May (Scotland Act 1998, s2(2)). The Parliament
is dissolved at the start of the 20 days ending on polling day, not counting
weekends, Good Friday, Easter Monday and Scottish bank holidays (s2(3); the
Scottish Parliament (Elections etc.) Order 2015, article 84 as amended in 2025,
and schedule 2, rule 2). The same count from the 2026 poll gives 8 April 2026,
Session 6's recorded last day from SPICe, so the rule is checked against the one
session held under it. Copies of the three pages are in `sources/legislation/`.

**It sits in a cell of its own, never in the last-day cell.** The real last day
is treated as fact: a bill that fell at dissolution is checked against it, and
promotion writes provenance from it. An estimate there would be checked as if it
were fact, and "empty means the session is still running" would stop being true.
The database requires the estimate on a session with no last day and refuses it
on one that has one, so when Session 7 ends the real day goes in and the
estimate comes out in the same change. Nothing already recorded reads it: no
bill was touched, and the error checker, the gaps list, loading and promotion
are unchanged.

**What a reader is told:** M14, and one sentence at the top of chart 5. The
provenance note cites legislation.gov.uk, read 17 September 2026, and says the
date is worked out rather than stated.

**What would reopen it:** the poll moved by proclamation, an early election, a
clash with a UK general election, or the rules changing. The date is then worked
out again, and M14 with it.

## 2026-09-17 — The published copy: finished figures, what crosses, how it is refreshed, and its date

**The owner's decisions**, groundwork 1.

**Every figure is worked out when the copy is taken**, not when a page opens.
The numbers change only at a refresh anyway, so a finished figure is the one
thing shown, downloaded and checked, and a shared link cannot change between
refreshes. *What would reopen it:* the chart switches adding up to more
combinations than it is sensible to work out in advance. **The owner's rider:**
nothing built rules out a figure worked out when a page opens; if one ever is,
it uses the same single calculation and shows it, and this is reopened for that
figure.

**What crosses.** In: session dates and notes, the methodology notes, the
provenance notes, each fact's source with its place and the day it was read,
what each code means, our own bill number, and the thin columns (procedure,
title at introduction, day a stage was reached). Out: stage record numbers,
which are reissued at every re-promotion; our created and last-changed times;
party, empty for all 470 bills; and the staging sheet, which holds introducers'
names as printed and which both source licences exclude. **The owner's rider:**
when a slice adds data, such as party, what crosses is decided again for it.

**The calculations already built carry over, and the charts are worked out from
them**, never from a second version written beside them; one a chart needs and
they lack is added in the same place. In a download, worked-out figures are a
file of their own, marked as worked out in the codebook with their source
columns and rule, and the calculation travels as text. **Left open, by the
owner:** whether our charts are *always* worked out in the database, the page
only drawing. The owner will decide once they have seen every calculation the
charts need, which exist and which are new; a bill's session quarter, for
chart 5, is the first case of a new one.

**The layout, as a starting point:** three files, each one line per thing —
bills with their stage dates across, stages with everything about each, and the
days between stages. Words in the cells, not codes; plain lower-case column
names joined by underscores, shown to the owner when built; the methodology
notes rewritten in those names at the same time, each changed note to the owner
in full.

**Refreshed only when new data is added or data changes**, at the owner's word,
run by a session, never automatically after a promotion. Rebuilt whole beside
the live copy and put live only if every check passes: cell by cell against the
working database, every figure re-run, the download rebuilt; one script, no
step by hand. The previous copy is kept, served to nobody, until the next
refresh, which makes the undo one step. A dated list of what changed is
published: a value already published is listed cell by cell with its old and
new value, which keeps no archive and so breaks no promise. **The owner's rider
on storage:** additions are listed as a count, so a large slice such as Official
Report data does not swell the list; the size of the list and of the kept copy
is reported at each refresh.

**It holds two things the working database does not**: the date it was taken,
and the list of changes.

**Every page and download carries the day the copy was taken.** The day each
source was read stays in the provenance; a download's readme also gives the day
it was downloaded; no "next update" date.

**The site's login to the published copy only reads**, proved by a check, as its
inability to open the working database was. **No action on heavy use**: pages
hand over finished numbers.

## 2026-09-17 — The download: CSV, one zip, and the date alone

**The owner's decisions**, groundwork 2, questions 1, 2 and 4.

**CSV alone to start**; another format only where the owner knows researchers
want it. Dates written year-month-day; the readme gives each file's row count.
**The owner's addition, as a starting point:** a link on the download page for
requesting another format, opening the reader's own email and storing nothing
on the site. A form was weighed and not chosen, since it would hold data about
people; the owner may come back to it as the site matures.

**One zip**: a plain-text readme, the three CSV files, a codebook, the
methodology notes, the provenance notes, the calculations as text, the list of
what changed, a suggested citation, and the licence and source statements. The
codebook is to the UK Data Service's minimum and generated from the published
copy's own descriptions. The readme names the Comparative Agendas Project's
"Scottish Bills" as a related dataset, in one sentence, with no comparison.

**The date alone identifies a download**, in its file name, readme and
citation; no release number. The readme says no earlier version is kept and a
researcher who needs one keeps their download. **The owner's words:** "we are
not offering to be a time machine"; managing a dataset over time is the
researcher's job, and good researchers are used to it.

## 2026-09-17 — The licence: our work under CC BY 4.0, each source's data under its own terms

**The owner's decisions**, groundwork 2, question 3, taken with an approach
meant to hold as the site takes data from many sources.

- **What the project made is under CC BY 4.0**, commercial use allowed, no
  share-alike: our coding, worked-out figures, methodology and provenance notes,
  our own bill numbers, and the owner's PhD compilation, credited to the thesis.
  The site says plainly that we are not responsible for what people do with the
  data, which the licence's own terms also say.
- **Each source's data stays under that source's terms, and its restrictions are
  passed on** in the source's own words, not interpreted. This sets aside the
  third draft's proposal to license the whole dataset: a CC BY licence over the
  Parliament's facts could grant a freedom that is not ours to give. The site
  says plainly it is not the Parliament's.
- **The statements follow each value's recorded source**, not a hand-kept list
  of columns, so they hold where a column mixes sources.
- **No source's data is published until its terms are written down**: licence,
  credit line, restrictions, link. The download and the site's sources page are
  built from that record. How and where it is held is put to the owner at the
  build, as an addition.

**The PhD dataset has no terms of its own.** The owner: it is theirs to use as
they please, and all of it was collected from Scottish Parliament sources. So
its values are Parliament facts under the Parliament's licence, and their
provenance credits the dataset too.

**The archived Scottish Parliament Licence 2017 was read**, through the owner's
browser, and kept in `sources/licences/`. It differs from today's in its credit
line and in carrying only the narrower party-political and advertising ban.
Every Scottish Parliament value, Sessions 1–5 included, is credited under
today's licence, and today's broader ban is passed on.

**The owner's decisions.** Every page showing data and every download sits

check follows any change to how downloads are served. Every page showing data
credits the sources its figures use, from the same record of each source's
terms.

## 2026-09-17 — The charts: a table of every bill, drawn on the machine, and two switches

**The owner's decisions**, groundwork 3.

**A table of every bill is on the list**, as the place a reader arrives from a
figure and as the house style's test. It is a lot of data, so how it is shown
gets a write-up of its own. A page per bill waits.

**Charts are drawn on the machine when the copy is taken**, as finished images
with their numbers in a table beneath; nothing is drawn in the reader's browser.
The tool is put to the owner by name. **Kept under review, at the owner's
asking**, for performance: drawing time at a refresh, size as switches multiply,
and readers finding a fixed image wanting.

**Two switches, the owner's**: leaving out bills of a given kind, and whether an
average takes every bill that reached a stage or only those that passed. No
other unless a methodology note requires one. Mean and median are both in the
table; which one a chart draws is the owner's call in its write-up. **The
owner's rider:** the switches need constant attention, since readers may need
more flexibility.

**Groundwork 3 opens with the list of every calculation the charts and the table
need**, which exist and which are new, and what each holds.

## 2026-09-17 — Showing the working: the page, the calculation, the date, and a reader who cannot see a chart

**The owner's decisions**, groundwork 4.

**A figure's page runs**: the figure; its rule in a plain sentence with its
notes; the sources; the date; the calculation, folded away. A reader goes from a
figure to the bills in it, and from a bill to its provenance notes. **Every
cited source has a copy kept**; a page names the kept copy where an address has
gone, and addresses are checked at each refresh. Only the fact sheets, two
procedure pages and the 2017 licence are kept today; the Official Report and
legislation.gov.uk pages are work for the build, put to the owner then.

**Each figure's calculation lives in one file**, which the refresh runs and the
page shows, and a check proves the two identical. **It is shown on the site,
with no link to GitHub.** The owner expects to make the repository private: it
holds the site's build, and the methodology and data reach readers through the
site; no build collaborators are expected. Checked: nothing depends on it being
public.

**The date in words** on every page and download, wording to the owner in full;
**the date inside a chart saved as an image**; and a page links to the list of
changes for a reader arriving by a shared link.

**Each chart has a CSV beneath it** carrying its numbers, sources, date and
page address. **A reader who cannot see a chart loses nothing**: the table holds
every number, the title, rule, sources and date are text on the page, and the
image carries a one-sentence description.

**The style is tested on the deployed table of every bill, with no separate test
page and no interim stage.** This changes the 15 September house style decision,
which promised a page "built locally and never deployed". The owner's reason: we
are the only users (checked 17 September: the owner's is the only account), and

## 2026-09-16 — The machine's checks run whoever is in the accounts, and prove they touched nobody else

**The owner's agreement**, on the task `STATE.md` set: the apply, sign-in and
admin checks refused to run once anyone but the owner had an account, so the
first real application would have ended them. They now take the privacy check's
shape: refuse only if their own invented people are already there, and delete
exactly those.

**Added, because a check that can approve, refuse and delete now runs beside
real people:** each fingerprints everyone else before and after — who they are,
their state, when it was decided, whether they are the owner — and passes only
if nothing changed. It prints yes or no, never a row. Someone real applying in
the seconds a check runs fails it; that is the safe way round.

**The admin check no longer keeps the admin screen on disk**, even for the
seconds it runs, because the screen lists real people.

**Not done:** the fingerprint does not cover codes or devices, since the owner
signing in elsewhere would fail it for nothing; approving, refusing and deleting
all change what it does cover. Rehearsal and results: `docs/ACCOUNTS-RUNBOOK.md`,
"The three checks, with real people in the accounts".

## 2026-09-16 — The privacy page: what it says, who it names, and where it sits

**The owner's decisions**, on `docs/PHASE-1-WHAT-IS-HELD.md`, which holds the page
word for word. Settled, and built and live the same day (`docs/ACCOUNTS-RUNBOOK.md`,

**One page, at `/privacy`, linked as "Privacy" in the header of every page**,

reason: there is nothing to fear or hide, so it should be easy to reach, not

**It names the owner**, as Dr Steven MacGregor, owner and administrator, with
`comparativelegislativedata@gmail.com` as the contact. **This is an exception to
the 16 September sign-in decision**, which said the owner's own details go into
no commit or document: a name on a public page is written into the page, and so
into the public repository. The owner chose to publish it. Nothing else about
the owner goes into the repository by this exception.

**Resend is named; the machine's host and the backup's storage are described by
what they do and not named.** Their names stay in the private notes, as before.
Cloudflare is left off, since no visitor's traffic passes through it.

**Rights and complaints:** a copy, correction or deletion on request at the

below, because it says a deletion is gone from the backups within five weeks.

## 2026-09-16 — The backup is separated by theme

**The owner's direction**, on finding that the accounts shared a snapshot with
the bills and so were kept up to ten years: separate what is backed up by theme,
even at the cost of a more complicated backup. The proposal is
`docs/PHASE-1-BACKUP-THEMES.md`; its four recommendations were taken.

**Three themes, three snapshots a night, one store.**
- **System**: `/etc` and `/usr/local/sbin`. Kept 14 daily, 8 weekly, 12 monthly,
  10 yearly, as before.
- **Data**: the working database. Kept the same.
- **Accounts**: the accounts database. Kept 14 daily and 4 weekly, so nothing
  older than five weeks. Shorter was possible; its cost is that a mistake in the
  accounts noticed after the last copy has gone cannot be undone, which with a
  handful of accounts means the person applies again. *(Carried from the
  proposal when Phase 1 closed.)*

Each database theme carries the logins, so either restores without the other.

**One store with three labels, not three stores.** Each store would need its own
password, and the password is already the one thing that, lost, makes the backup
unreadable. What would reopen it: wanting someone able to open one theme and not
another.

**A database not sorted into a theme goes into data**, and the job's log says
so. Nothing tells anyone when the backup fails, so refusing an unsorted database
would mean no backup at all, silently. The cost is that a future database about
people could be kept ten years. **The session sanity check now asks that every
database on the machine is sorted into a theme**, which is what catches it.

**Copies taken before the change:** only one data copy ever held the accounts,
and the only person in it was the invented practice applicant. The first run of
the new version replaced it as that day's copy and it was pruned. No data copy
on the storage box holds the accounts; each was listed to check.

**Found while doing it: the backup's own password had no copy off the machine.**
The owner held the storage box's login, which is a different password. Lose the
machine and the backup could not have been opened by anyone. The owner now holds
a copy, proved to open the backup, with the same test refusing a wrong one.

**Rehearsed before installing**, against a throwaway store on the machine
(`tools/rehearse_backup_themes.sh`): three copies each holding only their theme;
each database restored alone with counts matching; 210 back-dated copies aged,
the oldest accounts copy left 17.6 days, the system and data copies kept exactly
as the earlier rule keeps them; a version putting the accounts in with the data
caught; the installed version still running, so the undo works. Then installed,
run, and each theme restored from the storage box. The whole of it is in
`docs/ACCOUNTS-RUNBOOK.md`.

**Still open, and the owner's:** nothing alerts anyone when the backup fails.
Three themes are three things that can fail silently.

---

## 2026-09-16 — The admin screen, the three emails, and everything switched on together

**The owner's decisions**, on `docs/PHASE-1-ADMIN-AND-EMAIL.md`, taken as
proposed. The file holds every word of the screens and emails.

**The admin screen** is the owner's account's alone; anyone else is told there is
no such page. Waiting applications oldest first, accounts below, each with the
details given. Approving is immediate, being undoable by deleting. Refusing and
deleting each ask first on a page of their own, being undoable by nothing. The
owner's own account cannot be deleted from it. Its pages tell browsers to keep
no copy.

**The email goes first.** Approving and refusing each send one; if it cannot be
sent, nothing changes and the screen says so. Nobody is approved untold, and no
refused application is deleted before the person has been told, which is what
"deleted once they have been told" requires. Deleting an account sends nothing.
A refusal gives no reason.

**The emails** come from `no-reply@legislativedata.org`, with replies going to
the address the apply page gives; plain text, and no tracking of opens or clicks
(Resend's own settings for the domain were read and both were already off).

**The key the site sends with can only send, and only from
legislativedata.org.** The key held for the project had full access to the
Resend account, which the site has no need of. The owner makes the sending key;
it reaches the machine without passing through the conversation and sits beside
the code key, outside the backup.

**Asking for a code.** Only an approved address is sent one, at most three an
hour, and the page is the same in every case. To count them, a code's row is
kept for an hour after it was made; it stops working as before. That, and that
no one stays refused, are the two descriptions `db/accounts/002` changes, and
the only change to the accounts database.

**Switched on together**, once all of it has passed its checks: applying,
signing in, and the admin screen. The two switches are taken out, not flipped.
From then on anyone who finds the site can apply; the owner decides every
application.

**Found while building.** The page after asking for a code shows the address
filled in. Sending the browser on to that page with the address in the page's
own address was the obvious way, and would have written the address into the
access log, which holds nothing about a visitor. The page is shown directly
instead.

## 2026-09-16 — Signing in: the owner's code comes from the machine and is typed where everyone's is

**The owner's decisions**, on the seven points of `docs/PHASE-1-SIGN-IN.md`,
which holds the pages word for word.

**The owner's way in without email.** A command on the machine makes a code for
the owner's account and no other, and shows it. The owner types it on the
ordinary page with their address. There is nothing on the site only the owner
can use, so there is no back door to find: the same code, page, checks and
limits as a code sent by email. What it costs, and accepted: the code appears
in the conversation, where it lasts 15 minutes and works once.

**A code** is six digits, works once, within 15 minutes, and stops after five
wrong tries. When a code does not work the page says the same thing whatever
the reason, so it tells nobody whether an address has an account. Limiting how
often codes can be asked for belongs with the email step and is put to the
owner then.

**A key on the machine for scrambling codes.** A six-digit code kept as a plain
scramble could be worked out from the database in under a second, which would
make the database's own description ("reading this database does not let anyone
sign in") untrue. The key is a file only the site and root can read, outside the
repository and deliberately outside the backup: losing it only stops codes made
in the last 15 minutes.

**Being signed in** is one cookie, set only on signing in: 30 days, not readable
by the page's scripts, sent only over https, and withheld by browsers from other
sites' forms. The top bar says who is signed in and offers signing out, which
removes this device's marker and nothing else.

**What is live after this step:** the code page and signing out. The page that
emails a code is built and off until email is.

**The owner's own details may be given in the conversation.** `CLAUDE.md`'s rule
that real data about a real person goes into no conversation was written for
applicants, who have not agreed to that. The owner, giving their own details,
has. They still go into no commit or document, the repository being public; they
are in the accounts database only. This corrects the 15 September entry, which
said the owner's address lives in the private notes: it was never put there.

**One thing not built, found while building.** A check that refuses forms whose
browser says they came from another site was written and taken out before it
shipped. The site tells browsers never to pass on where a reader came from, and
under that setting browsers mark this site's own forms as coming from nowhere,
so the check would have refused every sign-in. The cookie's own setting is what
protects a signed-in person.

**The apply page's second sentence after applying is amended** (point 7): "If
that address is already waiting for a decision or has an account, nothing has
changed", because a refused person applying again now does make a new
application.
