## 2026-09-16 — Applying for an account: what the page does, what it keeps, and a refused application is deleted

**The owner's decisions**, on questions and wording put in
`docs/PHASE-1-APPLY.md`, which holds the page word for word.

**What applying does.** It sends no email: nobody has yet proved the address is
theirs, and an email on applying would let anyone use the site to send mail to a
stranger. The first email a person gets is the decision. A second application
from the same address shows the same page as the first and changes nothing,
whatever state the first is in, so that the form cannot be used to find out
whether someone has an account. The owner is not emailed about new applications;
the admin screen shows what is waiting. What would reopen that: applications
sitting unread.

**What it keeps, and for how long — new, not settled on 15 September.** An
approved application is kept while the account exists. **A refused application
is deleted once the person has been told.** It is the least that can be held,
and a refused application has no further use. What it costs: someone refused
and applying again is not recognisable as having been refused. It also means no
person stays in the refused state; the column's description changes to say so
when the admin screen is built.

**Where to ask for deletion:** `comparativelegislativedata@gmail.com`, given on
the page. Public by the owner's choice. An address at `legislativedata.org`
forwarded by Cloudflare was offered and not taken.

**What the page does not say.** A sentence promising that beta accounts would
get the data when it is published was cut: what an account gets is not settled.

**Against bots:** a hidden field, and nothing else. No captcha, which is a third
party; no limit by address, which would mean recording addresses, ruled out the
same day; no cookie, since an anonymous form gains nothing from one.

**It stays off on the live site until the admin screen exists**, so nobody
applies into a queue nobody can see. The machine turns it on; when the admin
screen goes live the switch is taken out, not flipped.

**Found with it:** `STANDING.md` and `PLAN.md` still said web server logs are
kept 14 days. Since "The site records nothing about a visitor" the log holds
nothing about anyone and is kept by size. Both corrected.

---

## 2026-09-16 — The accounts are built: the site cannot see the bills, and the backup takes every database unless told not to

**Built on the owner's go-ahead** to the plan put at the start of the session:
the accounts database first, in the nightly backup and proved restorable, before
any page that lets someone apply. The shape below was chosen in building it and
is recorded so it can be reopened, not because the owner weighed each part.

**What it holds is the list of 15 September and nothing more**: a person (email,
name, title, position, applied/approved/refused and when); a code, lasting 15
minutes and working once; a signed-in device, lasting 30 days. The database
refuses a code that lasts longer or a sign-in that does, so the limits are not
only in the site's code. **A code and a device marker are kept only as a
one-way scramble**, so that reading the database does not let anyone sign in.
**Deleting a person deletes their codes and devices with them**, which is the
owner's "delete an account and everything attached to it" made into a property
rather than a step to remember.

**The website's login cannot open the working database.** PostgreSQL lets any
login on a machine open any database unless told otherwise; that was taken away
from `legdata`, and tried. This is what the three-database decision was for — the
site unable to see the working data, not trusted not to look. No existing login
was affected.

**The website cannot make anyone the owner, or change an email.** It is given
permission column by column: it may add an applicant and record a decision, and
nothing else about a person. The owner's account is set on the machine, as
decided on 15 September.

**The backup takes every database on the machine, unless one is named as left
out on purpose.** The alternative was a check that complains when a database is
missed. It was rejected because **nothing tells anyone when the backup fails**:
a complaint would reach nobody. A database left out by mistake is the failure
that has already happened once; a database backed up by mistake costs disk.
When the published database exists it is named as left out, being rebuilt rather
than restored.

**Proved, not observed.** Made under another name first, checked as the site,
shown to fail when given a permission it must not have, undone, undone again,
then made for real. The backup was run and then **restored from the storage box**
into scratch databases, where an invented practice person was found approved and
the dataset's counts matched. The practice person was then deleted. The whole of
it is in `docs/ACCOUNTS-RUNBOOK.md`.

**What would reopen it.** The owner preferring the site to hold a record of who
approved or refused and why, which nothing holds now; the rules for codes
changing (attempt limits are counted per code); or the backup being given
somewhere to report failure, at which point a missed-database check becomes
worth having as well.

**Left open, and in `STATE.md`:** nothing alerts anyone when the nightly backup
fails. It predates today; today is when it was noticed.

## 2026-09-16 — Traffic comes straight to the machine; Cloudflare holds the name only

**The owner's decision, after asking what proxying would actually buy a project
this size.**

**What was chosen.** `legislativedata.org` resolves to the machine and readers
connect to it directly. Cloudflare is the registrar's DNS and nothing more — the
records are set to DNS only. Caddy gets the certificate from Let's Encrypt
itself and renews it without being asked.

**What was rejected, and it is not nothing.** Putting Cloudflare's proxy in
front would absorb a flood of traffic before it reached a machine that runs the
site and the database together, would let us rate-limit the apply form and the
sign-in codes at the edge, and would hide the machine's address.

**Why not, for now.** Those are insurance against traffic this site does not
have and may never have. Set against them: Cloudflare would decrypt every
request, which from Phase 1 onwards includes sign-in codes and which pages a
named researcher reads, and it would keep its own record of who visited that we
could not filter the way we filter our own. And the caching that makes a proxy
worth having is a specific hazard here — every page carries the date of the data
it was built from, and a cached page shows that date after it has stopped being
true, silently, which is the one failure the site's whole claim cannot survive.

**What would reopen it, and it is not a matter of taste.** Traffic we cannot
absorb, or someone attacking the site. It is one toggle at Cloudflare, and what
goes with the toggle is written down in `docs/DEPLOY-RUNBOOK.md` — Full (strict)
mode set before flipping, the first certificate renewal watched, the caching
rule decided, and the page saying what is held about a user amended to say that
Cloudflare now holds a log of visits.

**A note on order, which is the part worth keeping.** Grey first is not a
compromise between the two options; it is the only clean order whichever one you
end up at. Caddy gets the first certificate directly, and from then on renews it
itself. Starting proxied puts Cloudflare in the middle of that first handshake
for no gain.

---

## 2026-09-16 — The site records nothing about a visitor

**The owner's decision.**

**What it holds.** The access log records the page asked for, the time, how long
it took and the result. No address, no browser string, no headers. Nothing in
it distinguishes one reader from another or one visit from the next.

**Why.** Phase 1 is the first time this project holds data about a person at
all, and the rule it already runs on is to hold as little as it can. An address
is data about a person. The alternatives were considered and are recorded here
because they are the obvious things to reach for later: keeping addresses for a
week to see where abuse comes from, and keeping them indefinitely, which is what
every web server does unless told otherwise. Both were rejected on the same
ground — they create something about readers that we would then have to explain
on the page saying what is held about a user, protect, and delete.

**What it costs.** If the apply form or the sign-in codes are ever abused, we
will see that it is happening and not where from. That is accepted. The machine's
own protection against people attacking the way in is unaffected and separate.

**Where it is enforced, and the mistake worth not repeating.** One filter,
defined once in the global block of `deploy/Caddyfile`. It was first written
inside the main site's own block, which looked correct and was not: the `www`
redirect and the plain-`http` redirect are separate blocks and were not covered.
Within eight seconds of the ports being opened, a scanner probing for `.env`
files had its address written to the system journal. A filter that covers most
of the ways in covers none of them. The runbook carries the two commands that
check it, and they are run after any change to the logging.

---

## 2026-09-16 — The accent has a light value, because one value cannot serve both

**What changed, against the letter of the style decision of 15 September.** That
decision says there is one accent and only one: `#7ea8e8`. On the light
background it measures 2.4 to 1 against the page, where 4.5 is the floor for
text anyone is expected to read. It is not a preference; the links are not
legible. Light mode uses `#2f6cc4`, which measures 5.0 to 1, and `#24559b` for
the accent on hover, where dark mode has `#96b9ee`. *(The hover value added when
Phase 1 closed; it was in the stylesheet and nowhere else.)*

**Why this does not reopen the decision.** The accent is still one thing meaning
one thing — you can act here — and it still never touches data. It now has a
light value and a dark value, which is exactly what the other twelve tokens
have, and for the same reason. What the 15 September decision was refusing was a
second accent doing a second job, and there is still no such thing.

**Kept here rather than in the working style file** because a later session
looking at two hex values where the record says "one accent" would otherwise
reasonably conclude it was a mistake and change it back.

---

## 2026-09-15 — The site is written in Python, and what would make us change that

**The owner's decision, with a condition attached that is part of it.**

**What was chosen.** Pages are built on the machine and sent as finished HTML.
Caddy in front, which gets and renews the certificate itself; then gunicorn,
Flask, Jinja templates and psycopg. Everything is in Debian or pip. There is no
build step: a deploy is copying files and restarting, and the undo is copying
the old files back.

**What was rejected, and it was a real contender.** SvelteKit, which is what the
owner's own essays site runs on, and which would have meant one stack across
both projects. Phase 2's goal — researchers building their own tables and charts
without leaving the site — pulls towards it, because that is an application
rather than a document.

**Why not, and the reason is not that Svelte is worse.** It is that this
decision is cheap to reverse and the ones it would be traded against are not.
Phase 1 is seven pages of forms and prose. If a later phase wants a front-end
application, rewriting seven pages is a day's work and the database — the actual
product — never moves. Choosing the larger stack now to serve a phase not yet
scoped is the speculative build this project's own rules forbid. The price
avoided is concrete: a second runtime on the machine to patch, a build step that
can fail halfway and that the written undo would have to cover, and a few
hundred packages on a project whose rule is to ask before adding one.

**What it does not close off.** Charts, sortable and filterable tables, and the
user data builder tool are all buildable on this. Svelte compiles to a plain
JavaScript file that can be dropped into a single page; what is ruled out is
SvelteKit being the whole site, not Svelte being part of a page.

**One argument that cuts our way specifically.** A researcher needs to cite a
table — to link to it with those variables and those filters and have the link
still work in a footnote in five years. Pages built on the machine with real
addresses do that by default. A JavaScript application has to be made to, and
usually is not.

**The condition, in the owner's terms, and it is not a footnote.** *"The stack
does not support it"* is never a reason to cut or shrink a feature. If that
sentence is said, what is on the table is the stack, not the feature. Also
reopens it: more than a couple of rich interactive pages, or any later phase
finding a tool harder to build because of this choice.

**The machine, checked before deciding:** Debian 13, Python 3.13.5, PostgreSQL
17 listening only to itself, fail2ban and unattended upgrades. No Node and no
web server, so neither option was cheaper by inheritance. 139GB free and 11GB of
memory; size is not a constraint.

## 2026-09-15 — Prose runs narrow, tables run wide, and the data date sits inside the screenshot

**No left rail.** The essays site has one because a reader is inside a project.
This site has one dataset and nothing to be inside, so a single bar across the
top carries it.

**One page, two widths.** Prose runs in a reading column of about 700px. A table
is allowed out of it and may take the full width. Locking 470 bills into a
reading column is how a data site becomes unusable, and running prose the full
width of a monitor is how it becomes unreadable.

**Where the data date goes**, settled against the rule of the same day that
every page carries the date of the data it was built from. It goes in **two**
places: quietly in the footer of every page, and again at the top of any page
showing data, beside the heading, in muted sans.

**The reason for the second one is the whole reason.** A footer date is cropped
out of a screenshot. Someone pulling a table into a paper takes the table and
the heading, and the date has to be inside that crop or the figure travels
without its date.

## 2026-09-15 — Colour means one thing, and an outcome is a word

**The question was not which colours.** The ramp and the single accent come with
the house style. The question was what colour is allowed to *mean* once there is
data on a page, which is a decision about the research rather than about the
look.

**The accent means "you can act here", and nothing else.** Links, the selected
thing, the bar beside the important thing. It never touches data. A chart
palette, when Phase 2 has something to plot, never reuses it — so nothing on a
chart looks clickable.

**An outcome is a word, never a colour.** No green for passed, no red for fell.
Three reasons:

1. **There are more outcomes than colour can carry** — passed, fell, withdrawn,
   rejected at Stage 1, rejected at Stage 3, blocked, still before the
   Parliament.
2. **Colouring them makes a judgement.** A Member's Bill falling, shown in red,
   reads as failure. It is an ordinary outcome and the data should not editorialise.
3. **A word in a cell can be cited. A colour cannot.**

This leaves the interface almost monochrome, which is what the house style
already is.

## 2026-09-15 — Who the site is designed for, and the two questions a page must pass

**Designed for someone who will cite it** — a quantitative researcher on
legislation, a PhD student, a SPICe researcher, a journalist doing it properly.
Design for them and the person checking a single fact is served as well. Not
designed for someone to be impressed.

**The reader is the one who arrives when there is data.** An earlier framing had
Phase 1's pages persuading strangers to apply for beta access; the owner
corrected it — nobody is expected to apply until there is data on the site. So
Phase 1's handful of pages are held to the same test rather than to one of their
own, and they are looked at by the owner and whoever they invite.

**The test, two questions held against every page:**

1. **Could a reader see where this came from, when, and what we do not know —
   without asking us?** This is the project's standing principle that provenance
   reaches the reader, turned into something a page passes or fails.
2. **Is anything here to impress rather than to inform?** If yes, cut it.

**Why this pair and not a better-sounding one.** `PHASE-1.md` had already named,
independently, the trap this phase has to survive: one chart on the welcome page
to make it look like something. The second question catches it without anyone
having to remember the rule. A test that catches a trap already identified on
other grounds is likely to be the right test.

It also makes "professional, not flashy" something that can be applied: flashy
is not a look, it is anything present for effect.

**The owner is the sole tester in the early stages**, and that is accepted. The
one thing it costs is feedback on dense tables before Phase 2, and the answer to
that is under the house-style entry: a page built locally and never deployed,
carrying a real table of all the bills, to test the style against the hardest
thing it will have to hold.

## 2026-09-15 — Dark by default, and light as a setting from the outset

**The owner's decision, against a recommendation.** The recommendation was to
default to light, on the grounds that a research resource gets printed and
screenshotted into papers, that a dark page screenshotted into a white document
looks broken, and that most browsers strip the background when printing so a
dark page prints as pale grey text.

**The owner's answer, which holds:** people will view the data on the site or
download it. The screenshot-into-a-paper route is not the main one.

**What was settled:** dark is the default, and light is a setting from the
outset, done the way the essays site does it — a Mode control offering Dark and
Light.

**Two things built in rather than argued, because they cost nothing now and are
expensive later:**

- **Colours are named tokens, never hex values written into pages.** This is
  what makes "start with dark" mean what it says: light stays possible without a
  rebuild.
- **A print stylesheet that prints dark on white**, whatever the screen is
  doing, so a printed page is not pale grey text.

**Noted against Phase 2, not settled now:** a chart downloaded from a dark site
has to work wherever it is pasted. Charts exporting light while the site stays
dark is the likely answer.

## 2026-09-15 — The house style comes from the owner's own site

**Where it came from.** A list of other people's sites was offered — political
science datasets, legislative trackers, statistical agencies, reading-led
magazines — and the owner did not like most of them. They pointed instead at
their own side project, `essays.stevenmacgregor.uk`, a workspace for developing
a piece of writing. It is where "professional, not flashy" already exists in a
form that values can be read off, and it was adopted as the starting point.

**The two projects share a starting point, not a dependency.** Both begin from
the same tokens; each is free to move as its purpose requires; this site does
not track changes made to the other. Said plainly because "similarly styled"
otherwise decays into "was similar in September 2026".

**What is being taken is the structure, more than the values.** The essays site
has a twelve-step warm neutral ramp and a layer of names on top of it saying
what each step is *for* rather than what colour it is — the page, a panel, a
card, a border, body text, muted text, a heading. Light mode redefines the
twelve and nothing else changes; no page knows which mode it is in. That is why
the light setting costs almost nothing.

**Two typefaces doing two jobs.** IBM Plex Sans for the machinery — navigation,
labels, buttons, the small grey metadata lines. IBM Plex Serif for the
substance. On the essays site the research question is set in serif at 18px and
is instantly the most important thing on the screen without being large or
coloured. Ours is direct: sans for the site, serif for the bills.

**The 14px body splits by job.** 14px sans stays for the machinery —
navigation, labels, metadata, table cells, where it is right. Prose goes to
17–18px serif. The test is a methodology note: M2 runs to 5,140 characters and
is not a 14px read.

**Devices taken with it:** hierarchy from colour and weight rather than size;
actions as small underlined text links rather than buttons; hairline rules
between sections rather than a box around everything; empty states written as
sentences; and a note on a screen saying what it does *not* yet do. That last
one matters most to us — for a resource whose product is data with known gaps,
it is worth more than the colours are.

**How it gets tested before Phase 2.** One page, built locally and never
deployed, carrying a real table of all the bills — long titles, empty cells, the
lot — to test the style against the hardest thing it will have to hold.
`PHASE-1.md` forbids data on any page; the reason it gives is publishing a
figure before the rules for publishing exist, and nothing here is published, so
it does not bite.

**The observed values are in the site's stylesheet**, `site/static/css/site.css`,
so that nothing has to be read off the essays site twice. *(Until Phase 1 closed
they were also in `docs/PHASE-1-STYLE.md`; every value there was checked present
in the stylesheet before it was deleted.)*


## 2026-09-15 — The owner's account is the superuser, and applications are managed on the site

**The owner's decision.** Approving and refusing beta applications happens **on
the site**, on an admin screen the owner's account can see and no other account
can. It is not done by a session running something on the machine.

**This is not new scope.** "The owner can approve or refuse an application" was
already what Phase 1 delivers. What was settled is that it happens in the site
rather than behind it, which had been left ambiguous.

**One account, not a system of roles.** The owner's is the only account that
sees the screen. Anything more general is speculative and is not built.

**Whose account it is, is not written here.** The address lives in the private
notes outside this repository, under `CLAUDE.md`'s rule that real data about a
real person goes in no document and no commit message. This entry is the case
that rule was written for.

**Two things that follow:**

1. **The first account cannot be applied for**, there being nobody to approve
   it. It is created directly on the machine, which is the same route as the
   owner's way in that does not depend on email.
2. **The admin screen shows applicants' names, addresses, titles and
   positions.** It is a page of personal data about other people, and being
   reachable by no other account is a property of it, not a nicety.

## 2026-09-15 — What access becomes after beta is deliberately deferred

**The owner's decision**, and the reason it is recorded rather than simply not
discussed. Whether a download stays behind a sign-in once beta ends, or the
resource opens to anyone, is not answered now and does not need to be.

**What it changes.** `PLAN.md` and `PHASE-1.md` both had it as a question that
must be settled before Phase 1 closes. It no longer is, and both are amended.
The infrastructure discussion closes on four questions, not five, and style
opens when they are recorded.

**Why deferring it is safe here**, when this project's standing rule is that
"not yet built" is not a state a decision may be left in. That rule is about a
change to how data is coded, where a half-settled method leaves data half-coded.
Nothing is built either way by this one: Phase 1 puts no data on any page, so
there is no download to put behind anything. It is a question about what the
resource is for, and it is better answered with a working site and some
researchers using it than in the abstract.

**What reopens it, and it is not optional:** beta ending. It has to be settled
before the gate it describes is removed or kept, and before Phase 2 publishes
anything to anyone who is not an approved beta user.

## 2026-09-15 — No passwords; what is held about a user, in full

**The owner's decision**, closing the third infrastructure question and the
domain with it. The principle is the one the question was opened on: settling
what is held is settling how little we can get away with holding.

### Signing in

**There are no passwords.** Somebody asks for a code, it arrives by email, and
it signs them in. **The owner's proposal**, from having used it elsewhere.

**Why it is better here, and not only tidier.** It means we hold nothing secret
about anybody at all — no password to store, to leak, or to reset — and the
email address is proved by the act of receiving a code, so the separate step of
confirming an address disappears too. Less built, and less held.

- **A code lasts 15 minutes and works once.**
- **A device stays signed in for 30 days.**
- **Signing out on a device is in Phase 1**, and matters more than it would with
  passwords, not less: a 30-day sign-in on a shared or library machine needs an
  ending, and this audience uses shared machines.

**It adds no company.** Applicants have to be emailed either way to be told they
are approved or refused, and a password site needs email for resets. What
changes is that email becomes load-bearing for every sign-in rather than for
exceptions. **So the owner needs a way in that does not depend on an email
arriving** — not a back door on the site, a way in from the machine itself. That
is a Phase 1 build item.

**Known friction, named before rather than after:** university mail systems
filter aggressively, and this audience sits behind the strictest of them.

### What is held

**Because the site cannot work without it:** an email address; which state they
are in — applied, approved or refused; and the dates those happened.

**Because the owner has to decide something:** name, title and position. **The
owner's judgement**, and it is narrower than was proposed — a free-text line on
what the data was wanted for was offered and declined. What would reopen it:
title and position turning out not to be enough to approve or refuse on.

**Because it cannot be avoided:** a sign-in code, for 15 minutes; a marker on
the device, for 30 days; and web server logs, **kept 14 days and then gone**.
The logs are the part that gets forgotten — they record every visitor's address,
they are personal data, and they accumulate nightly whether anyone decides about
them or not.

### What is never held

- **A password**, there being none.
- **Anything about what a signed-in researcher looked at.** We have no use for
  it and a reading log sits badly beside maximum transparency.

### Who else sees it

**Resend**, for sending. A new API key is to be generated; the notes record an
account and key from a previous attempt and neither is to be assumed live.
Resend will see every user's email address. That is a third party holding
personal data, which is a thing we declined a free tier over — it is necessary
here in a way it was not there, because there is no sending without a sender,
and **the privacy page names them plainly rather than leaving it implied.**

**Cloudflare**, managing DNS for the domain. To establish when the site is
built: whether traffic is proxied through them or DNS only, because that decides
what the web server sees and therefore what is in the logs.

### What follows, as build items rather than notes

1. **A short plain-English page saying exactly what is held** — the list above,
   and who else sees it.
2. **A way for the owner to delete an account and everything attached to it.**
3. **A way for the owner to get in that does not depend on email.**
4. **The accounts database in the nightly backup before the first real account
   exists**, rehearsed like a promotion.

### The domain

**`legislativedata.org`**, already held by the owner from before this project,
already connected to Resend for sending, DNS through Cloudflare. Settled.

### Considered and parked

**"Sign me out everywhere else."** Not needed now. What would reopen it: an
account being shared, or a device being lost and the 30 days mattering.

## 2026-09-15 — Every page carries the date of the data it was built from

**The owner's decision**, closing the one point left open inside the
three-database decision taken the same day. Every page showing data carries the
date of the data it was built from. The owner's reason: maximum transparency.

**It is a rule, not a nicety, and it does two jobs.** For a reader it is what
makes a figure citable — they can say what they saw and when it was true, and
come back to it. For us it is the thing that makes a stale published copy
visible. A copy that has silently not been refreshed for three months is the
failure this shape is most exposed to, and a date on every page means anyone
looking at any page can see it, including us.

**It follows from what we already said we vouch for** — the data as it stands
when it is accessed, stamped with the date it was taken, settled 2026-09-15.
This is that promise made good on the page rather than in a document.

What would reopen it: nothing foreseen. A page that cannot show a date is a page
whose data came from somewhere this decision has not placed.

## 2026-09-15 — Three databases: the working one, the published one, and the accounts

**The owner's decision**, closing the second infrastructure question. The
briefing it was taken from is `docs/PHASE-1-WHAT-THE-SITE-READS.md`, which dies
with the phase.

**The shape.** Three separate databases, all on the machine the site runs on:

1. **The working one** — the staging sheet, the clean sheet, the methodology
   notes, the provenance. Everything sessions are loaded into, promoted on and
   rolled back on. Unchanged by this decision. Not reachable from the site.
2. **The published one** — takes from the working one only what is published,
   when we choose, after a promotion we are satisfied with. This is what a
   reader's page reads.
3. **The accounts** — read and written directly by the site, because a password
   changed at 2pm cannot still be the old one at 2.05. Never mixed with bills.

**Why three databases rather than three sets of tabs in one.** Separation is
what lets the site's way in be unable to *see* the working data at all, rather
than being told not to touch it.

**Why the published one is not simply the working one.** Not exposure — the
floor and the hosting decision had already dealt with that. The risk left was a
reader's visit straddling a promotion: nothing they see is ever half-finished,
because promotion is a single all-or-nothing action, but a figure read at 2.10
and a figure read at 2.20 can disagree with nothing on either page admitting the
ground moved. That is silent, which is what makes it worse than corruption.
Reading a copy taken at one moment means every figure in a visit agrees with
every other, and the date it was taken can be shown and cited.

**Why "only what it needs" is doing real work.** The published one holds no
staging sheet and no unadmitted candidates. A reader cannot see unreviewed data
by accident, because it is not in the building.

**Backups.** The working one and the accounts are backed up; the published one
is not, being rebuildable from the working one in seconds, and a copy of a copy
raises the question of which is authoritative on a restore. The nightly backup
goes off-site to the Hetzner Storage Box, which is what makes three databases on
one machine safe — the machine is a single point of failure and the backup is
the thing not on it.

**The gap this opens, and it is a Phase 1 build item.** The nightly backup dumps
one database and will not pick up a new one by itself. The accounts database has
to be in the backup on the day the first real person has an account, not noticed
afterwards, and it is rehearsed the way a promotion is: back up, restore into a
scratch copy, confirm the account is really there. Between 2026-09-09 and
2026-09-10 nothing backed up the database at all, because the backup was
skipping a directory that no longer existed and succeeding quietly every night.
That is the failure this item exists to not repeat.

**What this costs, recorded rather than discovered.** Refreshing the published
copy becomes a step in the promotion runbook, with a rehearsal and a written
undo like every other step.

**Still open within this decision:** whether every page carries the date of the
data it was built from. It was put to the owner as part of the briefing and has
not been answered. It matters because it is what makes a stale copy visible to
everyone including us, which is the failure this shape is most exposed to.

**Not closed off:** writing the published data out as files at promotion time
and having the site read no database for bills at all. At 304 kB of bills it is
viable, and the published copy is the natural thing to write those files from.
It cannot be settled until the style discussion says what a reader's tools are.

## 2026-09-15 — The front end runs on the machine we already rent

**The owner's decision**, closing the first infrastructure question. The site
runs on the machine the database is already on, not on a provider with a free
tier. In the owner's words: it keeps everything self-contained, and it keeps the
database safely off the internet.

This also answers `PLAN.md`'s question of whether the site and the database
share a machine. They do.

**What the comparison turned on.** Phase 1 puts no bill data on any page — it
builds a welcome page and a way in. So the thing being hosted is not pages about
bills; it is a page that remembers people, and it is the first time this project
holds anything about a real person. Free tiers are built to hand out pages that
do not change and do not remember anyone. A login is the opposite, so that
option was not one new company to depend on but two — one to run the site, one
to keep the accounts — with real people's details sitting at the second from the
first day there were any.

**The reasons, in the order they carried weight:**

1. Nobody new to depend on, at the moment the project starts holding data about
   real people.
2. Those details stay behind our own firewall and inside the backup that already
   runs nightly.
3. It costs nothing more. The machine is prepaid for a year and is paid for
   because the bills are on it.
4. It keeps the Phase 2 door shut. Site and bills in one place means the bills
   never travel and no door is opened for them.

**The price of it, recorded so it is not discovered later.** We own the running
of it: security updates, the certificate that makes the padlock appear, the web
server in front of the site, and the response when something stops at night.
Automatic security updates are already on. If that job ever becomes one the
project should not own, that is the reason that would reopen this.

**What it would take to undo.** Everything on the machine is ours and copyable,
and no part of the site is to be written in a form only one company can run.
Moving means renting another machine and putting the same things on it.

**One consequence of the two sharing a machine**, worth knowing rather than
acting on: a single prepayment lapsing now takes down the data and the site
together. The renewal date matters more than it did.

The comparison this was decided from is `docs/PHASE-1-HOSTING.md`, which dies
with the phase.

## 2026-09-15 — The working database is never reachable from the public internet

**The owner's decision**, agreed before the hosting question was taken, and it
constrains every answer after it. Whatever the site runs on, the database that
sessions are loaded into, promoted on and rolled back on is not reachable from
the public internet.

**Why it was settled first, and separately.** It is a floor, not a choice
between options. Where the site runs can be got wrong and put right — if the
machine turns out to be the wrong one, we move it. Exposure cannot be put right
the same way: a working database that sat open to the internet for six months
has already been open for six months, and no later decision undoes it.

**What it does not settle.** Whether the site reads a copy of the data or the
working database itself, from inside the machine, is the second infrastructure
question and is still open. The floor rules out one thing only: the working
database being reachable from outside.

## 2026-09-15 — Infrastructure is settled before style, and they are separate discussions

**The owner's decision**, opening Phase 1: the two scoping discussions are kept
apart and run in order — infrastructure first, style after it, with
infrastructure closed before style opens.

**Why the order is that way round.** Where the site runs, and what it reads
from, decides what can be built on it. Style settled first would be settled
against an unknown and re-argued the moment infrastructure moved under it.

**The two infrastructure questions the owner names as the main ones**, in this
order:

1. **Where the front end runs** — the machine we already rent, or a provider
   with a free tier. `PLAN.md`'s separate question of whether the site and the
   database share a machine is folded into this one; it is the same question
   asked from the other end.
2. **What the site reads from** — the working database directly, or a copy taken
   from it, with the working database not reachable from the site at all.

The three remaining questions from `PLAN.md` — what is held about a user, what
the beta gate becomes after beta, and the domain — are not dropped and still
have to be settled before the phase closes.

**The second question gets a written briefing before the discussion, not during
it.** The owner has said plainly that they are not an experienced database
developer and want to be guided on safe practice here. A guide delivered
mid-conversation is a guide nobody can weigh, so it goes in a file and the
discussion happens after it has been read. What it has to cover is listed in
`docs/PHASE-1.md`.

**Guiding is not settling from inside the project.** `PLAN.md` requires both
discussions to take in views from outside rather than be answered from within,
because this project's habits were built for a hand-made dataset of 470 bills
and are not evidence about how to run a website. That rule is against quietly
adopting whatever is convenient. It is not against explaining the options: the
session brings them, costed, with what each risks and what published practice
does, and the owner decides.

## 2026-09-15 — Every phase gets a plan, and closing the phase destroys it

**Proposed by the owner**, reviewing `PLAN.md`: "each phase gets a detailed plan
so that we can work methodically but one of the close down requirements is that
we throw it away and only retain what is essential (ops, infra, decisions etc)
in the main plan or other relevant docs."

**Why it is the right shape for this project.** `PLAN.md` is the arc and has to
stay readable, but a phase needs working detail to be built methodically — the
order of things, what is being tried, what turned out not to work. Those are
opposite requirements in one file. Splitting them is the same move that produced
`STANDING.md` and that keeps `STATE.md` to a screen. The phase plan is where the
detail is allowed to be long, precisely because it has a death date.

**Deleting it is safe.** The file stays in the repository's history. What
deletion removes is its presence in the places people read, which is the point:
this project's failures have been second copies rotting in plain sight —
`VARIABLES.md` drifted for five days — not things lost.

**The sweep has a fixed list of homes**, which is the part that makes it work
rather than an aspiration. Every line of a phase plan is a settled decision
(`DECISIONS.md`), a standing position or a verified fact or something
deliberately left undone (`STANDING.md`), how to run or undo something (a
runbook), what a table or column holds (a `COMMENT`, so it reaches the data
dictionary), a change to the arc (`PLAN.md`), or working detail — and working
detail goes. "Keep what is essential", decided at the end of a long session, is
the instruction that let `STATE.md` reach 942 lines.

**Nothing is cut until it is proved present in its new home**, by the rule
already used for moving data and for the 261 lines that became `STANDING.md`.

**The sweep is run by a session that did none of the phase's work.** It is part
of the closure test, which a different session already runs, and whoever wrote
the phase plan is the worst judge of which of their own notes are essential.

**It is not for the owner.** The owner orients from `STATE.md`. A phase plan
collecting status would be a second `STATE.md` growing where nobody cuts it, and
that is the failure mode this decision has to avoid.

Phase 0 closed without one and is not revisited. The first is `docs/PHASE-1.md`.

## 2026-09-15 — What we vouch for is the data at the time it is accessed

**Decided by the owner**, reviewing the plan: "users are responsible for their
citations. We do not guarantee historic downloads. Users can download copies of
the data if they want but beyond that we only vouch for accuracy AT THE TIME IT
IS ACCESSED."

**The position.** Every figure and every download the site publishes carries the
date it was taken. We do not keep an archive of superseded versions, and we do
not undertake to serve one. A user who needs a fixed version downloads it and
keeps it; the stamp is what makes their copy citable, and the citation is
theirs.

**Why it is right rather than merely convenient.** The Parliament states that
historical records may be revised, and they have been. A resource promising a
retrievable version history would be promising something its own source does not
offer, and would have to decide what a "version" of a revised record even is. The
honest offer is the current data, dated, with the route back to what said so —
which is the standard this project was already held to.

**What it is not.** It is not a refusal to version the data. The reader can
always tell which version they are holding, because it is stamped. What is
refused is the archive, and the undertaking to serve from it.

**Where it lands.** `PLAN.md` carries it as the third thing that makes the
resource research grade, alongside provenance reaching the reader and decisions
being transparent rather than correct. Its concrete form is a Phase 2
deliverable: the stamp on every download and every chart, and public wording
saying what it means. That wording is not yet written and goes to the owner
verbatim when it is.

## 2026-09-15 — The plan reviewed, and six gaps closed

**The owner asked for a fresh analysis of `PLAN.md`** rather than a defence of
it, and settled every question it raised in one pass. What changed:

**Where the site reads from is an infrastructure question, and the first one.**
The plan placed the site without saying whether a reader's page looks at the
working database — the one sessions are loaded into, promoted on and rolled back
on — or at a copy taken from it when we choose. Phase 0's whole discipline is
the staging sheet against the clean sheet; the site is a third surface and was
unplaced. It now heads the Phase 1 infrastructure questions, to settle in the
scoping discussion before anything is built.

**What a logged-in person sees in Phase 1 is now written down:** a welcome, that
they are logged in as themselves, change password, log out. Nothing else. This
adds one screen to the phase — the password change was not in it before — and
in exchange it removes the argument the phase was most likely to lose, which is
one chart on the welcome page to make it look like something. The "must not" now
names that temptation.

**Style is a deep dive, and the bound moves.** The plan had "the first stylistic
decisions are taken", which can absorb unlimited work. The owner's answer was
that style deserves real time, so the bound is no longer on what gets decided
but on what gets built: Phase 1 builds those pages and nothing else, whatever
the deep dive settles. Phase 1 scoping is two discussions, infrastructure and
style, both taking in views from outside this project.

**The dataset stays as it is while the site is built.** One bill is before the
Parliament and the data grows very slowly, so freezing it costs almost nothing —
but a phase-at-a-time plan implies that silently, and what a plan implies is
what gets argued about later. Now stated. A screen for entering new data joins
the candidates at the end, as the owner's screen rather than a researcher's,
explicitly not a priority, and named so nothing in the site is built in a way
that makes it hard to add.

**Phase 2 closes from a second account**, not the owner's. Phase 0's closure
rule was that the tester did none of the work it tested; the site's version of
that is a reader who is not the person who built it.

Recorded separately, because it is a standing position rather than plan detail:
what we vouch for is the data at the time it is accessed.

## 2026-09-15 — Indexes, not copies, and standing material leaves `STATE.md`

**Decided by the owner**, on being shown a proposal that included exporting the
methodology notes to a file: "Shouldn't instead we have an index which we can
refer to rather than duplicating the material which will — i guarantee — just
lead to drift!" They were right, and the proposal had failed to apply its own
argument: the same session had just refused to write a summary document on
exactly that ground.

**The rule.** Where a thing already has a home, the repository gets an index to
it, never a second copy of it. And the index is generated, because the line that
matters is not copy against no copy — it is hand-written against generated. A
generated document cannot drift, which is why the data dictionary is trusted.

**Built.** The data dictionary now carries an index of the methodology notes —
code, title, and the columns each bears on — from the same tool and the same
query. The bodies stay in the database, which is where they are published from.
This also fixes something that had been wrong for days: column descriptions said
"see methodology note M5" while pointing at nothing a reader could follow.

`DECISIONS.md` gained a contents block at its top, generated by
`tools/make_decisions_index.py` from its own headings — 102 decisions, each line
a heading copied exactly. Five thousand lines nobody reads is how a settled
decision gets taken again, differently. The tool writes only between two markers
and refuses to run unless both are present and in order, because this file could
not be rebuilt if it were damaged. Regenerating it joins the opening check.

**`STATE.md` was two documents, and is now one.** It held 942 lines, 807 of them
below the line. 261 of those were standing material — the owner's settled
positions, what had been verified rather than assumed, the reconciliation
figures, the tools, the connection procedure — sitting in a file whose whole
discipline is "if it grows, cut". Standing material in a file that gets cut
every session is material waiting to be lost, which is what the owner was
worried about when they asked whether a single document was needed.

They are now in `docs/STANDING.md`, with one section written new: what was
deliberately left undone, and what would reopen each thing. That is the actual
protection against reinventing a wheel — not a record of what was decided, which
`DECISIONS.md` already holds, but a record of what was considered and parked.

**The move was proved before anything was cut**, by the rule already used for
moving data: all 261 lines were checked present in the new file first.

**What did not happen.** No summary document was written. A document holding
"everything important about the dataset" would be a third copy of what
`DECISIONS.md`, the methodology notes and the dictionary already hold, and on
this project's own record — `VARIABLES.md` drifted for five days before it was
caught this morning — it would be wrong within a month, and wrong in the worst
way, because it would look authoritative.

## 2026-09-15 — Durations are calendar days, and `VARIABLES.md` is the reasoning, not the schema

**Two things settled, on the owner's challenge.** `VARIABLES.md` was the last
document still describing the database as it was several sessions ago, and the
proposal was to cut it back to the reasoning behind the variables. The owner
asked what would actually be lost, since presentation is about to begin and
ingestion will resume after it. Checking each section against `DECISIONS.md`
rather than assuming showed the answer was: mostly nothing, but not nothing.

**What the four documents each do.** `DATA-DICTIONARY.md` says what every column
is, and is generated so it cannot drift. A methodology note tells a reader what a
judgement was, and by the entry below does not say how we got there.
`DECISIONS.md` records each decision on its day. `VARIABLES.md` holds the
reasoning behind the shape of the variables and the questions still parked, and
nothing factual about the schema. A question settled there moves here.

**D3 is settled: calendar days now, sitting days later.** Recess makes calendar
days misleading and the Parliament's rules count some intervals in sitting days,
so sitting days are in one sense truer. They need a calendar of when the
Parliament sat, which is its own body of work and is not built; calendar days
need nothing beyond the dates held. So every duration published today is calendar
days and says so, and sitting days are added later as an alternative measure.

**Why that is safe to build on.** No derived measure is stored — every duration
is worked out from the stage dates when asked for, never written down as a
number. Adding a sitting-day measure later therefore changes nothing already
recorded. That rule was stated in `VARIABLES.md` from the start and is recorded
here because it is the rule the presentation layer inherits.

**Why it was not already here.** D3 lived only in an "open decisions" list as a
proposal, and `DECISIONS.md` assumed it in passing — one line about recesses
getting their own tab "when sitting days become a variable" — without ever
recording it. Three other things were in the same position: the rule above, the
financial resolution parked as a stage event, and the finding that the
Parliament's API returns truncated and duplicated records. All four are now
either here or kept in `VARIABLES.md` deliberately.

**Still open, and kept in `VARIABLES.md`.** Whether the financial resolution is
recorded as an event between Stages 1 and 2 — it can hold a bill up, so it may
explain Stage 1 to Stage 2 intervals that otherwise look odd. Revisit if those
figures turn out not to be explainable without it. A bill *falling* for want of
one is a separate matter and is already recorded.

**Found while checking.** The party column, settled on 10 September, is empty for
every bill: the first slice's two questions do not need a member, so it was never
filled. For bills introduced by a Law Officer and for Private Bills, brought by a
promoter, the empty cell is the right answer and not a gap to chase. Recorded in
`VARIABLES.md` against the slice that fills it.

**Nothing was written to the database.**

## 2026-09-15 — A bill only restated stays when the later session comes off

**Decided:** where a fact sheet lists a bill belonging to an earlier session and
changes nothing about it, taking the later session off the clean sheet **leaves
that bill where it is**. Where the later session wrote over cells of it, the bill
still comes off and its own session is promoted again to rebuild it, as it has
since `db/081`. Which case a line is in is recorded on the line when it is
promoted — `bill_candidate.continued_bill_cells_changed` — rather than worked out
afterwards. Built as `db/103`, with both tools changed.

**Why.** The Session 7 closure test found that taking Session 7 off took the
Gender Recognition Reform Bill with it. That bill belongs to Session 6 and
Session 7 changed not one cell of it. The owner: removing it would be rewriting
the past incorrectly. The full procedure did restore it — take Session 7 off,
put Session 6 back — so nothing was ever lost; the objection is that it is two
steps and the second is the one a person forgets, for a bill that never needed
touching.

**Why it is written down rather than worked out.** The answer could have been
read off the provenance notes, which name the fact sheet that changed each cell.
The owner was shown both and chose recording it: a number written at the moment
promotion knows the answer cannot drift, and deleting a bill is not a decision to
take on the strength of matching prose. The number is checked from both ends —
`db/103` filled the four existing lines by counting notes, and promotion, run
again over Sessions 5, 6 and 7 in a rehearsal, worked out the same four from the
staging lines and the clean sheet.

**Not a change to what the data says.** Nothing on the clean sheet moved, no
reader sees the new cell, and no methodology note was needed. What changed is
what an undo does.

**Where the rules on the new cell live, and why not the error checker.** It was
proposed for `v_candidate_problems` and is not there. That list is what the owner
reads when reviewing a session, and a missing internal number is not something
the owner can do anything about. It is held instead by two checks on the table
itself — a line that continues nothing may not carry a number, and a number may
not be negative — by promotion's own end-of-run checks, and by the undo refusing
to run when a promoted continuing line has no number. Stated here because it
departs from what was agreed before building.

**Mended at the same time, and not a decision:** the undo's own "about to
remove" table counted only the session being taken off, so it said one bill and
then removed two.

## 2026-09-15 — A bill still before the Parliament is counted, and has no ending

**Decided:** a bill the fact sheet leaves still before the Parliament goes on the
clean sheet like any other, with its outcome recorded as in progress and nothing
recorded about an Act. It is counted as a bill of its session. Where a chart
shows timescales by session, a session whose bills have not yet completed a
stage is shown **blank, with methodology note M13 against it** — blank meaning
there is nothing yet to measure, not nought days. Built as `db/102`, which adds
M13.

**Why.** Session 7 brought the first bill this database has ever held that has
not finished. Everything else about recording one was already in place and was
rehearsed against Session 7 before anything was written: the values exist with
definitions of their own, the loader sets them from the fact sheet's own table,
promotion carries them, the error checker asks nothing extra, and
`v_stage_date_gaps` already had an `in_progress` branch that asks such a bill
only for the stages below the furthest it has reached. The only missing piece
was the part a reader sees. M5 covers a bill that passed and was then stopped;
nothing covered a bill that has simply not finished.

**Which bills a figure about time covers is a front-end decision, and stays
one.** The owner's instruction, given while the note was being drafted: the
flexibility to cover every bill with any terminal point — a bill that completed
Stage 1 only, say — or only bills that completed every stage, must stay open,
because it is a decision about what to include and on what basis, not a question
about the database. The database was already built this way and
`v_bill_stage_durations` says so in its own description: a bill rejected at
Stage 1 carries a real introduction-to-Stage-1 period, with a flag beside it
saying the bill did not get through that stage, so that neither choice is built
in. The School Meals (Scotland) Bill's 218 days is the worked example.

**Two drafts of M13 were wrong and were withdrawn before it was applied.**
Neither was a fault in the data; both were the note overreaching, and both are
named in `db/102`'s header and in item 13 of Session 7's closure test so they
cannot creep back.

- The first said a count of bills and a count of bills with a recorded duration
  differ by the number of live bills. They do not, and already differed by 62
  before Session 7 existed: `v_bill_total_duration` measures introduction to
  *final* stage, so a bill that stopped earlier is not in it. The rehearsal's
  per-session counts showed this.
- The second said a bill that never reached its final stage has no timing figure
  either. That takes one view's scope for a property of the data, and would have
  written the front-end decision above into published methodology.

**Found by** rehearsing the promotion before writing the note, rather than
after. Neither error would have been visible in the note read on its own.

**Decided:** where promotion writes a provenance row for a bill's note, all

and 10 September. So each of the three rows said, in one breath, that the note

## 2026-09-15 — Two items of Session 6's test were wrong, and are rewritten

**Decided:** items 19 and 23 of Session 6's closure test are corrected, and the
corrections say what they first said and why it was wrong. Neither was a fault
in the data.

**Item 19** said all three uncarried Stage 3 dates were already on the bill with
the same date. Line 440's restates the Session 6 fact sheet's 23 May 2021
against bill 303's 23 March 2021 — which is the settled position of 2026-09-13,
not a discrepancy: the bill keeps the adjudicated date and the staging line keeps
what the document printed. The expected answer was written carelessly against
work already done and recorded in three places.

**Item 23** asked that no note on the clean sheet end in anything but `. ? ! "`
and cited `db/079` for it. `db/079` considered that rule and rejected it in

titles and web addresses. Run as written it returns four Sessions 1 and 2 notes,

actually settled: no provenance note's words end in "Read at".

**Why this is worth an entry.** A test that cites a migration for a rule the
migration declined is a test that will be believed. Rule 4 of the procedure says

## 2026-09-15 — A session is finished by its own closure test, not by seven tests of its parts

**The owner, on being told Session 6 was ready to promote:** "I remain deeply
concerned that we previously had a robust process for finalising the data for
each session which seems to have given way to a set of adhoc approaches."

It had, and it is visible in the files. Sessions 1 to 5 each have one closure
test in two parts — Part A mechanical, Part B the owner's sign-offs — written by
the session that did the work, run by a different one, with a
`closure_check_session_N.sql` beside it, and the session is not *closed* until
both parts are complete. Session 6 had no such test. What it had instead was
seven tests attached to pieces of work, each properly written and properly marked
by another session, and nothing that tested the session. Nothing in the project
would have said when Session 6 was finished.

Two smaller instances of the same drift, recorded here because they are the same
shape. The runbook's steps 6 to 9 — the comparison against the owner's dataset,
the Official Report on every fallen bill, legislation.gov.uk on every bill left
awaiting assent, and working the error checker's list to empty — were not written
down until 2026-09-14, after Sessions 6 and 7 had been loaded and announced as
ready for review without them. And the question of what happens to a bill's note
when a later fact sheet changes the bill was found on 2026-09-15 and parked on a
list headed "not blocking anything", when it was a question about how data is
coded on bills that day's promotion was about to change.

**What was decided.** Session 6 gets a closure test in the old shape — Part A
mechanical with the source of every expected answer, Part B the owner's
sign-offs, and `tools/closure_check_session_6.sql` beside it. It inherits the
seven piece-tests rather than re-arguing them. It is written by the session that
did the work and **run by a different session**, and Session 6 is not closed
until both parts are done. Session 7 will have the same.

**Why this is the rule rather than a preference.** The piece-tests were not worse
than the session test; several were more thorough. What they could not do is
answer the question "is this session finished", because none of them was about
the session. A test per migration measures whether each change did what it said.
A test per session measures whether the session's data is fit to be relied on.
The project needs the second and had been producing only the first.

## 2026-09-15 — A bill's note is the eighth cell a second appearance carries

**Settled with the owner on 2026-09-15**, in the parts a change to how data is
coded has to be settled in, before anything was built. `db/098` builds it and
`tools/promote_session.sql` carries it.

**The problem.** When a later fact sheet lists a bill already on the clean sheet,
promotion updated seven cells on that bill — title, the Act's number, whether it
became an Act, the Royal Assent date, the date it ended, how it was stopped
before Royal Assent, and what followed — and never touched the note. The note is
written in our own words at review, and the reasoning was that a script has no
business writing it. That is right about where a note comes from and wrong about
where it goes.

Session 6 is where it bit. The European Charter of Local Self-Government
(Incorporation) and UNCRC (Incorporation) Bills were passed in Session 5, stopped
before Royal Assent by a section 33 reference, and each carries a note ending
"it could not be submitted for Royal Assent in its unamended form". Both were
reconsidered and passed in Session 6 and are now Acts. Promoting Session 6 as
things stood would have written each Act's title, number and Royal Assent date
onto the bill and left that sentence standing beside them.

**The rule.**
- The note is carried like the other seven: a further appearance with a note of
  its own replaces the note on the bill it continues.
- An empty note on such a line means the earlier note stands, and promotion never
  blanks one. But the error checker asks for a note wherever the bill being
  continued has one, so leaving the earlier wording is a decision somebody made
  rather than something nobody noticed. Where it is still right it is repeated,
  which changes nothing and writes no provenance.
- Promotion writes the note's provenance as it does the other seven, keeping what
  it read before. That row says the note was rewritten at review, and its source
  is `manual`, not the fact sheet — the note is ours, and its provenance should
  not claim otherwise.
- M6 closes by telling a reader this.
- The four bills that appear in two fact sheets were rechecked. Three needed new
  notes and have them. The fourth, the Gender Recognition Reform Bill, needed
  none: its Session 7 line already carries the same note word for word.

**Why a check that only speaks when something is wrong was not enough.** The
alternative was a rule that flags a note contradicting the bill's own cells.
Nobody can write that rule for free text, and the same reasoning was rejected at
`db/090` a day earlier for the same reason: a check that goes quiet unless it
happens to recognise the fault is not a check. Requiring somebody to say what the
note should read is a question that always gets asked.

## 2026-09-15 — A methodology note says what the judgement was, not how we arrived at it

**The owner, reading M12 whole:** "Why such a detailed explanation for the simple
fact that we found the data to replace stale dates in the factsheet? Isn't that
all we are saying?"

Mostly it was. M12 ran to 290 words for a judgement that takes about ninety.
`db/097` cuts it, and retitles it *A fact sheet is a snapshot*.

**What was cut, and why none of it was load-bearing.** A second telling of "a
fact sheet is not a running record", which the first sentence already says. A
paragraph explaining in the abstract that the line came from the fact sheet while
particular facts came from legislation.gov.uk — a reader does not need that
argued, because every such cell carries its own note naming the source and the
day it was read. The list of the seven Session 6 Acts, which duplicates the data
and goes out of date the moment another session brings more. And a closing
paragraph on blocked bills, reduced to a clause pointing at M5, which is where
that case is actually explained.

**What stays, because a reader is worse off without it.** That the sheet is a
snapshot, with the seven Acts as the evidence that this is not hypothetical. That
every bill a sheet leaves awaiting Royal Assent is checked **and the answer
recorded either way** — the sentence that earns its place, because it is what
lets a reader tell "looked up, still no Act" from "never looked at", and it is
why the four blocked bills read blocked rather than unknown. And that where the
Act was made, its date, number and title come from legislation.gov.uk with the
day each was read.

**The general rule this sets, and the reason it is here rather than only in the
migration.** A methodology note is read by someone deciding whether to trust a
number, not by someone auditing how we got it. It should say what the judgement
is and what follows from it. The reasoning, the alternatives weighed and the
blind spots found belong in `DECISIONS.md` and the migration that made the
change, where a later session will look for them and a reader will not. M12 had
absorbed all three.

This settles how M12 is written. It does not settle anything about the other
eleven notes, and none of them has been looked at against it. Whether they
should be is raised in `STATE.md` as a question for the owner, not decided here.

**What did not change.** `applies_to` still names the same four cells. The
procedure in `PROMOTION-RUNBOOK.md` is untouched and still cites M12. The error
checker's complaint on an awaiting-assent line without a look-up citation still
says "see methodology note M12" and still means this note. The 290-word wording
is quoted in `docs/STATE.md` as committed at `ccac41c`.

## 2026-09-15 — A bill rejected at Stage 3 is recorded as that, not as a bill that fell

**The owner's ruling, 15 September, asked whether recording the Assisted Dying
and Recall of Members bills as Stage 3 rejections rather than as bills that
simply fell is the distinction the published data should draw: "Yes".**

The Session 6 legislation fact sheet says only "Fell" for all ten of that
session's bills that did not pass. `db/092` read all ten at the Official Report
and found the one word covering three different things: five bills whose general
principles the Parliament disagreed to at Stage 1, two the Parliament refused to
pass at Stage 3, and three that were never decided at all and ran out of time
when the session ended. Those are three different events, and the sixth item of
that migration's closure test put the Stage 3 pair to the owner because
`rejected_stage_3` had one previous instance in the whole database — the Budget
(Scotland) (No.2) Bill of Session 3, on the Presiding Officer's casting vote.

**So the distinction stands**, and nothing needs building: Assisted Dying for
Terminally Ill Adults is recorded as rejected at Stage 3 on 17 March 2026, on
motion S6M-21005 in the name of Liam McArthur, For 57 Against 69 Abstentions 1;
the Scottish Parliament (Recall of Members) Bill on 24 February 2026, on motion
S6M-20904 in the name of Graham Simpson, For 30 Against 66 Abstentions 27. Each
has its Stage 3 row marked as where the bill stopped, dated the day the
Parliament decided, and each quotes the Presiding Officer on the line.

**Why it matters for the research.** A bill the Parliament actively refused to
pass, after it had completed Stages 1 and 2, is not the same event as a bill
nobody ever voted on. Collapsing them would make "how long each stage took"
count a rejected bill and an abandoned one as the same kind of ending, and would
hide the only two occasions in twenty-five years on which the Parliament took a
bill all the way to a final vote and turned it down.

---

## 2026-09-15 — A stage a bill was in but never worked on is not a stage it reached

**The owner's ruling:** "It was passed Stage 1 and Stage 2 started but no formal
meetings on amendments were held and then the Bill timed out. I think that needs
to mean that the Bill only completed Stage 1 and that is the relevant date we
would be interested in. Had there been any amendments considered at Stage 2 that
would be different."

The Ecocide Bill and the Freedom of Information Reform Bill both completed
Stage 1 and then fell at Stage 2 when the session ended. `db/095` recorded them
identically but described them as different, having read the lead committee's
meetings listed under Ecocide's Stage 2 heading as Stage 2 proceedings on the
bill. They were not. Further down the same page the Parliament says so: "A date
for Stage 2 consideration of the Bill was not set prior to the dissolution of
Parliament. Marshalled List and Groupings documents were therefore not
produced." Amendments were lodged on 6, 10 and 24 February 2026 and never
considered. Freedom of Information Reform's page carries no such section and
lists no amendments at all.

**So both bills are recorded the same way: Stage 1 completed and dated, Stage 2
as where the bill stopped, with no date.** `db/096` corrects the two notes.

This settles the question `db/095` left open, and settles it by removing it:
whether a committee meeting date should be read as the day a bill reached
Stage 2 does not arise, because those meetings were not that. **M11 stands
unchanged** — the day a bill reached a stage is recorded only where a source
states it in terms, and is never worked out from anything else. The owner's
"had there been any amendments considered at Stage 2 that would be different"
marks where the line falls if a bill ever does reach proceedings and stop inside
them; no bill yet has.

**What this is really about.** A bill can sit at a stage for months without
anything happening to it. "How long each stage took" must not count that as
time in the stage, or every bill that ran out of time acquires a long Stage 2
it never had.

## 2026-09-15 — A check that says "nothing is wrong" must say whose fault it would be

`tools/load_phd_stage_dates.sql` refused to keep anything unless the error
checker was completely empty afterwards. That was written when the checker was
always empty between pieces of work, and it stopped being true the moment
something was left standing in it that nothing could answer yet: Session 7's
Gender Recognition Reform line cannot say which bill on the clean sheet it
continues until Session 6 is promoted. So the loader refused Session 6's 136
stage dates over a line in another session that they have nothing to do with.

**The check now compares the checker's findings before the load with its
findings after, and requires that the load caused none of them.** Problem by
problem, not by counting, so a problem disappearing while a new one arrives is
still caught. It was proved both ways before it was used on real data: it passed
Session 6's CSV, and refused the same CSV with one bill's Stage 2 date moved to
before its own Stage 1.

The general point, which is why this is here and not only in the runbook: a
check that asserts the whole database is clean will eventually block work for a
reason unrelated to that work, and the temptation then is to turn the check off.
A check that asserts *this change broke nothing* does not have that failure, and
is the stronger statement anyway.

---

## 2026-09-15 — A bill's second appearance is not asked for stages that belong to its first

`tools/phd_stage_dates.py` refused Session 6 over three lines, saying each had no
row in the owner's dataset: the UK Withdrawal from the European Union (Legal
Continuity) Bill, and the two bills the Parliament took back and passed after
reconsideration. The dataset is not missing them. A bill that appears in two fact
sheets has one row, under the session it was introduced in, and its Stage 1 and
Stage 2 belong to the line it continues — where they already are, on the clean
sheet.

`db/086` settled exactly this for the gaps list, which stopped asking a second
appearance for stages it already has. The reader now does the same: **it writes
nothing for a line that continues a bill already on the clean sheet.** It is not
a blind skip. It first checks that the bill being continued really does hold both
of its first two stages, and refuses if it does not, for the same reason the
excuse for a bill genuinely absent from the dataset is checked: a line quietly
excused is a line excused into a gap nobody will find.

Sessions 1 to 5 give byte-identical output from the reader before and after,
693 lines, which is how a change to it is tested.

## 2026-09-15 — A session is reviewed with its stage dates already on

**The owner's ruling:** "let's review with the dates added but happy to push that
back to another sesson."

Sessions 1 to 4 were reviewed and then had their stage dates typed on. Session 5
had its dates loaded first and was reviewed once, with everything on the sheet.
Nothing had ever chosen between the two; both happened. Session 5's way is now
the rule: **the owner reviews a session once, with its stage dates already on
the staging sheet.**

Why it matters beyond tidiness: the stage-date loader refuses a whole session if
any bill that did not pass has nothing saying where it stopped, so loading the
dates surfaces work that the review would otherwise have been asked to accept
without. Session 5 found six such bills that way, and Session 6 has fourteen.

Promotion stays last, and the dates are reviewed like everything else on the
sheet: nothing reaches the clean sheet unaccepted.

## 2026-09-15 — A bill that passed, was stopped and was then withdrawn, and the rule that gives

### The owner's ruling

"agreed." — to the proposal below, put to them with the alternative and its
consequence.

### The bill

The UK Withdrawal from the European Union (Legal Continuity) (Scotland) Bill
passed on 21 March 2018, was stopped before Royal Assent when the Supreme Court
ruled parts of it outwith the Parliament's legislative competence, and was
withdrawn on 10 March 2022. Its Session 6 line is a further appearance of bill
305 and says all three things at once, which no line had had to do before.

### Three rules, one of which had to give

- **Only a bill that passed can be stopped before Royal Assent.** So the cells
  saying the bill was stopped and then withdrawn cannot sit on a line whose own
  outcome reads `withdrawn`.
- **A completed Stage 3 means the bill passed.** The line carries a Stage 3 row
  dated 21 March 2018, read off the Session 6 fact sheet's own words.
- **A bill that passed with no Royal Assent date must be recorded as blocked or
  awaiting one.**

The first two stand and the third gives. It was written at `db/020`, before the
cells that say what followed a block existed at all (`db/084`). Its job is to
stop a bill that passed being recorded as never becoming an Act with nothing
saying why, and `assent_block_outcome` does that job better than the rule does.
It now accepts one more answer: *or the line says what followed the block.*

**The alternative, rejected**, was to leave the line saying the Parliament
withdrew the bill. Two rules would then complain, the blocked-bill cells could
not be filled, and — the deciding point — the clean sheet would go on recording
a bill withdrawn in 2022 as still waiting for Royal Assent, because
`assent_block_outcome` is one of the seven cells a further appearance carries
and `still_blocked` would never be replaced.

### The eight parts

1. **What it records.** No new variable and no new cell. Line 412's outcome
   becomes `passed`, and the two blocked-bill cells are filled: `s33_reference`
   and `withdrawn`.
2. **Which bills, and what empty means.** A line recording that a bill stopped
   before Royal Assent was later withdrawn. One line today. An empty
   `assent_block_outcome` still means the bill was never stopped.
3. **Where it sits on the clean sheet.** Bill 305 keeps `passed` — promotion
   carries seven cells onto a bill a line continues and `outcome` is not one of
   them — and stops saying it is still blocked.
4. **How it arrives.** By hand at review, from the fact sheet's own words.
5. **Promotion and provenance.** Unchanged. Promotion already writes a note for
   every cell a further appearance changes, saying what it read before and what
   it reads now.
6. **What the checker requires.** The one rule above, at `db/094`.
7. **What a reader is told.** Nothing new. **M5 already names this bill** and
   says it "was withdrawn on 10 March 2022, nearly four years after it passed".
8. **Every bill coded the old way, rechecked.** Two questions asked of the whole
   database: which lines have a completed final stage and an outcome that is not
   `passed` — one, this one; and which say a bill passed, give no Royal Assent
   date and are recorded as neither blocked nor pending — none, before or after.

### Raised, not settled

**M5 has drifted in two places** and was deliberately not touched. It says the
mechanism that stopped a bill is recorded in `bill.note`, where since `db/084` it
is also a cell of its own; and it closes by saying a bill's recorded state comes
from the latest fact sheet read in, which M12 now qualifies. Neither makes any
data wrong. M5 is text a reader sees, so any rewording goes to the owner in full
before it is made.

**The `withdrawn_from_earlier_session` section has no rule** tying it to an
outcome, where the Acts, Withdrawn, Fallen and awaiting-assent sections all have
one. One line has ever been read from it, and a rule written on one instance
would be a guess at the next.
